blocks.prompt: The Worm That Built the Ground
blocks.text: A worm has no eyes. It has no ears and no nose. So how does a worm know where to go? It feels. A worm can feel light on its skin. It can feel the ground shake when a bird lands. Then it slides down fast. A worm has no teeth either. It swallows dirt and old leaves. Inside, a hard pocket called a gizzard grinds the food up small. What comes out the other end is fresh new soil. Plants love it. Every worm in your yard is quietly making the ground better while you sleep.

blocks.prompt: A Machine Made of Rings
blocks.text: Pick up a worm and it feels like nothing but a wet noodle. It is not. A worm is a machine built out of rings. Look closely and you can see the rings, called segments. A big earthworm has about 150 of them. Each segment carries four tiny pairs of stiff bristles. You cannot see them, but you can feel them. Rub a worm gently backward along your finger and it catches like sandpaper. Those bristles are how a worm walks without legs. It grips the soil with the bristles at its back end, squeezes itself long and thin to push its head forward, then grips with the front and hauls the rest along. Long, short, long, short. That is a worm walking. The worm has no lungs. Air soaks straight through its wet skin and into its blood. That is why a worm must stay damp. A dry worm cannot breathe, and a worm left on hot pavement will not last the afternoon.

answers: segments
it grips the soil with the bristles at one end, stretches, then grips with the other end and pulls itself along
it breathes through its wet skin, and a dry worm cannot breathe
(inference: it can grip anywhere along its body, so any part of it can hold on while the rest moves)

blocks.prompt: The Sidewalk After the Storm
blocks.text: Here is a question with no settled answer: why do worms crawl onto the sidewalk when it rains? The usual explanation is that they are drowning, and that the burrows fill with water and force them up. It is a tidy story, and it is probably wrong. Earthworms take in oxygen through their skin, and that works fine in water. Some can survive submerged for days. Better ideas exist. A worm on dry ground dries out in minutes, so rain is the only safe time to travel any distance across the surface, and a worm looking for a new burrow or a mate has to travel somehow. Another idea is stranger. The drumming of heavy rain may feel exactly like a mole digging, and a worm that stays put when a mole is coming does not stay a worm for long. People who hunt worms for fishing bait use this. They drive a wooden stake into the ground and rub it with iron, and the ground hums, and worms come boiling out of the soil. It is called worm grunting. The moles, it turns out, taught them the trick. While we are killing myths, here is another. Cut a worm in half and you do not get two worms. The half with the head can sometimes seal the wound and grow a short new tail, if enough of it is left. The other half has no brain and no mouth. It wriggles for a while, which looks like life, and then it stops. So the sidewalk after a storm is not a graveyard of drowned worms. It is a road, and some of the travelers ran out of time when the sun came back.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.
items: The passage says the drowning explanation is probably wrong. What evidence does it give?

answers: worms take in oxygen through their skin, so water is fine, and some can survive submerged for days
a worm on dry ground dries out in minutes, so it can only travel far while the surface is wet
rubbing iron on a wooden stake makes the ground hum like a digging mole, so the worms flee upward
(inference: the worms were traveling on purpose, not dying by accident, so it is a journey rather than a disaster)

blocks.prompt: Darwin's Last Book
blocks.text: In 1881, six months before he died, Charles Darwin published his last book. It was not about finches or fossils or the origin of species. It was about worms. Darwin had been watching them for more than forty years. He kept them in pots in his study. He tested whether they could hear by shouting at them, by having his son play the bassoon at them, and by setting their pots on the piano. Shouting and bassoons did nothing. The piano, whose vibrations traveled up through the pots, sent them diving. Worms are deaf and they are not fooled. He tested whether they could think. A worm plugs the mouth of its burrow with leaves, and to pull a pointed leaf underground the sensible move is to grab the tip. Darwin found they usually did. So he cut paper triangles, which no worm had ever met, and offered those instead. The worms still mostly grabbed the pointed end. Something in that tiny animal was solving the problem, not just following a habit. Mostly, though, Darwin measured. He worked out that the worms under an English field could pass more than ten tons of soil through their bodies per acre per year, hauling it up from below and leaving it on the surface as castings. Everything lying on that field therefore sinks. Stones sink. Roman walls sink. Darwin laid a flat stone on his lawn and had his family measure it for decades as the worms buried it, and the thing is still there. That is the discovery, and it is bigger than it sounds. The layer of dark crumbly soil that every plant on land depends on is not just sitting there. It is being eaten, ground in a gizzard, and laid down again, over and over, by animals with no eyes and no bones. Darwin ended his book by pointing out that few animals have played so large a part in the history of the world, and he was not being sentimental. He had the numbers.

meta.templateLabel: The Worm That Built the Ground

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ecosystem engineer: it rebuilds its habitat
European worms came in ship ballast
Spreads about thirty feet a year
Strips forest duff within a few years
Darwin: forty years of worm study

blocks.prompt: The Worm Is Not Always the Hero
blocks.text: Everything you have been taught about earthworms is true, and in half of North America it is also a problem. Start with what a worm does. An earthworm is a tube that eats the ground. It swallows soil and dead leaves, grinds the mix in a muscular gizzard full of swallowed grit, absorbs what it can use, and voids the rest as castings that are richer in usable nitrogen and phosphorus than the soil that went in. Meanwhile the burrow itself does work. A nightcrawler's tunnel can run six feet straight down and stay open for years, letting rain and air reach roots that would otherwise sit in dense, airless dirt. The animal is a plow, a compost heap, and a drainage system, and it costs nothing, and there can be a million of them under a single acre. Ecologists have a term for a creature that rebuilds its own habitat on this scale. They call it an ecosystem engineer. So worms are good. That is the story every gardener knows, and in a garden it is exactly correct. Now go north. Push the map up into Minnesota, Ontario, Wisconsin, the forests that sat under a mile of ice twenty thousand years ago. The glaciers scraped those soils bare, and when the ice pulled back, the earthworms did not come with it. Worms are slow. Left alone they spread perhaps thirty feet a year. Those forests spent ten thousand years growing up without a single native earthworm in them, and they grew up strange because of it. A worm-free northern forest builds duff: a thick, spongy, slowly rotting mat of old leaves on the forest floor, sometimes a hand deep. That mat is the nursery. Sugar maple seedlings root in it. Trilliums and ferns and wild ginger live in it. Ground-nesting birds and salamanders hide in it. Nothing about that forest is built for an animal that eats leaf litter for a living. Then Europeans arrived, carrying soil as ship ballast and worms in the root balls of their apple trees, and later anglers began dumping leftover bait at the ends of lakes. European earthworms have been spreading through those forests ever since, and where they arrive, the duff goes. Not slowly. A worm invasion can strip the forest floor to bare mineral soil within a few years. The seedlings fail. The trilliums vanish. The salamanders decline. The soil that gardeners praise worms for building is, in that forest, the wreckage of something that took ten millennia to make. This is the part worth sitting with. The worm did not change. Its behavior in a Wisconsin woodlot is identical to its behavior in an English pasture: eat litter, mix soil, cast. What changed is the place, and whether the place had ten thousand years to grow around the animal or ten. Good and bad are not properties of the worm. They are properties of the fit between a creature and where it has been put, and we are the ones who keep moving creatures. Darwin, who spent forty years proving that worms had quietly built the ground under England, never saw this coming. He was not wrong. He was writing from inside a place where the fit was already old.
